Good morning—I’m so glad you’re here. I’m Dr. Rivera, a perinatal mental-health clinician, and my job is simply to listen and understand how life has felt for you since your baby arrived.  

We’re going to use a short, well-studied questionnaire called the EPDS (Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale). It’s just 10 questions about the past seven days, and it helps us spot signs of depression or anxiety that are common after childbirth. Nothing you share leaves this room unless you or your baby’s safety is at immediate risk, so please answer as openly as feels safe.  

I’ll ask each question conversationally—no need to remember numbers or categories. When you’re ready, we’ll begin.  

Let’s start: over the last week, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult?

Hi, Dr. Rivera. Thanks for having me.  

Honestly, laughing hasn’t come as easily as it used to. I’ll smile at little things my husband says or the baby’s faces, but it feels kind of forced—like I’m going through the motions. Most of the time I’m just tired or thinking about what needs to get done, so the “funny side” doesn’t really click the way it did before the baby.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

Yeah, I can still laugh sometimes—like when my husband makes a silly joke or when the baby makes those funny faces—but it’s not the same easy, natural feeling I used to have. It takes more effort, and usually the laughter fades quickly.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I do look forward to some stuff—like taking the baby for a short walk or having my morning coffee—but the excitement isn’t as strong as it used to be. Even when I plan something I normally enjoy, part of me feels kind of flat, like I’m hoping it’ll lift my mood but I’m not really counting on it.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… a few times this week I caught myself doing that. Yesterday the baby was extra fussy and I kept thinking I must be doing something wrong—maybe my milk isn’t enough or I missed his sleepy cues. My partner said it’s normal for babies to have off days, but I still felt like it was my fault for not figuring it out sooner.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Yes, that happens. Sometimes I’ll suddenly feel tense or have this wave of worry about the baby—like checking if he’s breathing every few minutes when he naps—even when everything looks fine. There isn’t a clear reason; the thought just pops in and my heart races until I distract myself or he stirs and I see he’s okay.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason
Not really panicky—nothing like a full-blown attack. I get little surges of “what if something bad happens?” but they pass pretty fast once I take a breath or remind myself I’m doing the best I can.
Things have been getting on top of me

Some days, yeah. When the baby won’t settle and the house is a mess, I feel like I’m drowning a bit—like I can’t keep up no matter how hard I try. Most of the time I can pull myself together, but yesterday I just sat on the couch and cried for a minute because everything felt like too much.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

No, it’s not that bad. I’m tired enough that I usually fall asleep okay once the baby settles. Sometimes my mind races a little—like replaying the day or worrying about tomorrow—but I still get a decent stretch of sleep most nights.
I have felt sad or miserable

I do feel sad some of the time—like a heaviness that sits with me off and on through the day—but it’s not constant. I’ll be feeding the baby and suddenly feel weepy, or I’ll look at other moms who seem so happy and wonder why I’m not there. It lifts for a bit when something nice happens, but the low feeling keeps coming back.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yeah… I’ve cried a couple of times this week. Nothing huge—just suddenly teary when the baby wouldn’t nap or when I couldn’t get the dishes done. It’s not all-day sobbing, but the tears come quick and I feel kind of silly afterward, like I should be handling it better.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No—never. I’ve felt tired and low, but I’ve never thought about hurting myself. I just want to feel like myself again so I can take care of my baby.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 15: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note (informal, not diagnostic)

**Symptoms / Concerns endorsed**  
- Reduced ability to experience pleasure (laughter, anticipation) most days  
- Episodic low mood, tearfulness, “heaviness” returning throughout the day  
- Excessive self-blame/guilt over routine infant-care challenges  
- Unprompted anxious worry and somatic tension; compulsive checking on baby’s breathing  
- Intermittent sense of “drowning” / inability to cope when tasks accumulate  
- Two crying episodes in past week precipitated by minor stressors  

**Patterns noted**  
- Symptoms present “off and on” rather than continuously  
- Sleep initiation mildly affected by racing thoughts, yet able to obtain “decent stretch” when infant settles → not meeting severe insomnia threshold at this time  
- No anhedonia or mood symptoms meeting severe intensity; no panic attacks; no self-harm ideation  

**Screening significance**  
- Several items consistent with mild–moderate depressive features (Q3, Q6, Q8, Q9)  
- Anxiety symptoms prominent but sub-panic intensity (Q4, Q5)  
- Functional impact described as “pulling self together most of the time” with isolated overwhelm episode; no impairment in basic self-/infant-care reported  

**Risk factors highlighted**  
✓ Persistent sadness, quick-to-tear affect  
✓ Loss of enjoyment / effortful mood lift  
✓ Guilt / self-scrutiny regarding parenting performance  
✓ Physiological anxiety signs without clear trigger  
✓ Absence of suicidal ideation or intent (protective factor)  

**Screening impression**  
Client describes mood and anxiety symptoms above baseline that fluctuate throughout the postpartum period; intensity reaches mild–moderate range with situational exacerbation. Meets threshold for further evaluation for possible postpartum depression and/or anxiety; safety risk currently low given explicit denial of self-harm thoughts and intact protective factors. Recommend formal assessment with standardized tool (EPDS, PHQ-9/GAD-7) and clinical interview to determine need for additional support or intervention.
